articles.title: Which current three-loss team would be the most dangerous in this year's College Football Playoff?
articles.summary: Oregon, South Carolina, Ohio State, Ole Miss and LSU all have three losses, but one team stands out as the most dangerous CFP contender this year.
articles.body: It's November, which means we are rapidly approaching the end of the regular season in college football. Two weeks from Saturday, the 2026 season will come to a bittersweet end, followed by conference championship weekend and then, finally, Selection Sunday for the College Football Playoff the very next day. With that in mind, and reading the tea leaves from the first few CFP ranking reveals, it seems as though this year may be the year we finally see a three-loss team making an appearance in the Big Dance. CFP REACTION: ALABAMA FEELS THE LOVE, INDIANA GETS THE SHAFT AND BIG 12 GETS RELIEF AS COMMITTEE CONFUSES US That sight will be much more commonplace after next year when the field expands to 24 teams, but a three-loss playoff team in the 12-team era is certainly unprecedented. But who has the best shot of going on a run out of all of the three-loss teams logjammed in the middle of the CFP rankings? To my eye, there are five teams sitting between 16 and 21 that have three losses as well as a legitimate shot at making the cut: Oregon, South Carolina, Ohio State, Ole Miss and LSU. I realize there is a good chance more teams join this list, but as of right now, these seem to be the most likely candidates from the pool of three-loss teams. I considered adding Missouri to the mix, but the Tigers have Georgia and Kentucky lurking these next two weeks, and 1-1 in that two-game stretch feels optimistic at best. Plus, their best win is over a reeling Florida team, so I'm not sure they would have much of an argument unless they took down the Bulldogs this Saturday. Ole Miss and LSU are both interesting cases. The Rebels have arguably one of the best quarterbacks in college football in Trinidad Chambliss and a damn good running back in Kewan Lacy to boot. Ole Miss also has a couple of really nice wins over LSU and the aforementioned Missouri. NEW COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF POLL PROVES THE SELECTION COMMITTEE IS JUST MAKING IT UP AS THEY GO LSU is a bit more of a stretch. As I mentioned, they lost head-to-head against the Rebels and really don't have a great win on their resume outside of a drubbing to open the season against Clemson. Their offense is always dangerous thanks to the play calling combo of Lane Kiffin and Charlie Weis Jr., and they have one of the most expensive rosters in college football. One thing both of these teams have going against them, though, are very recent blowout losses to superior conference teams. The Tigers just got done getting dominated in the fourth quarter by a surging Alabama team, and the Rebels were completely manhandled by Georgia just six days ago. The Bulldogs look like the best team in the country, so that may be excusable, but Ole Miss also has a loss to Florida on their resume in which they were completely outclassed for the majority of the second half. Moving on to Ohio State and South Carolina, both of these teams are dealing with some high-profile injuries. Ohio State lost its signal caller, Julian Sayin, for the remainder of the 2026 regular season and potentially beyond. They haven't looked the same without him, and picked up their third loss at home against Oregon last Saturday. You could make an argument South Carolina is one of the hottest teams in the country, with head coach Shane Beamer going from hot seat to en fuego. The Gamecocks are riding a four-game winning streak into the end of the season, and have a seriously impressive victory over Tennessee to pad their case. The loss of dynamic QB Lanorris Sellers and big-play wideout Nyck Harbor changes that calculus a bit, as it's unclear what the long-term outlook is for either of the South Carolina stars. That leaves us with Oregon, who I believe is far and away the most dangerous three-loss team left standing. The Ducks looked shaky early in the season, but look like a completely different team since firing their offensive coordinator in late October. Dan Lanning's squad put up 41 points just last weekend against a very salty Ohio State defense and seem to be peaking at the right time with Dylan Raiola leading the charge under center. They also have a much more forgiving final stretch (Michigan, at Michigan State, and Washington) while also having impressive wins against Ohio State and likely Group of 6 playoff representative Boise State. They've been able to shake off the loss of their star quarterback Dante Moore, and this was a team that was being picked by many to win the whole thing back in August. That talent hasn't gone anywhere, it's just taken a while to get off the starting blocks. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Do I think Oregon is a shoo-in to win the whole thing? No. I'm not even sure if they'll be in the field come December. But if they do manage to sneak into the CFP, they will be entering the tournament playing a blisteringly hot brand of offense that no one will want to see lining up on the other side of the field. A three-loss team is almost guaranteed to find its way into the field of 12 this year, and if Oregon is that three-loss team, I wouldn't count them out from making a very deep run.

articles.title: FAA issues nationwide ground stop on all departing flights, citing 'communication issue'
articles.summary: FAA issues a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the United States.
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights in the United States until further notice, "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."

This means that planes currently in the air may land, but those on the ground may not take off.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters Friday evening that there is currently no reason to suspect a national security threat is behind the communications outage affecting flights.

"There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for their loved ones," Mullin said.

"This is not another 9/11," he added. "This is a telecommunications outage; this is much different."

Mullin said it would "take some time" to resolve the issue and that flights already in the air are being handled on a "case-by-case" basis.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a post on X , "The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

As of 6 p.m. ET, there were over 10,000 flights delayed and over 1,700 canceled within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware.com , a live flight tracker website.

There were more than 30,000 departures and arrivals scheduled for the remainder of the day, according to flight tracking app Flighty, the New York Times reported .

Airlines for America, an industry trade organization representing major U.S. airlines, wrote in a post on X , "Safety is always our top priority." It added that it's in communication with the Department of Transportation and the FAA. The association encouraged travelers to be in touch with their airline carrier for "real-time updates."

Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation into the nationwide ground stop.

"The safety of our skies is built on redundancies," she wrote on X in response to Duffy's update. "Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation. As Aviation Subcommittee Ranking Member, I'll be demanding answers from the FAA."

The cause of Friday's widespread communication issue is still unclear.

"Do we know what has caused it yet?" Mullin said. "No, we're going to go through it. But I'm not going to make assumptions."

Microsoft said that its own global outage — from which it is still recovering — did not appear to be a factor.

The National Weather Service told the New York Times that a screenshot going viral online claiming that its weather radar is down is "outdated," adding that it "has not experienced a disruption to its radar systems today."

Earlier this week, the FAA announced the nationwide rollout of a new $875 million artificial intelligence tool to help air-traffic controllers avoid delays. Called SMART — short for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — it was made by an AI company called ASI and had previously been in use at Washington, D.C., airports since late September.

On social media, ASI said "the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."

A Yahoo reporter who is currently on the tarmac on a United Airlines flight waiting to depart from Los Angeles International Airport passed along updates from the cabin. She said her pilot said that "what happened was a communications outage that started in Kansas City Center, which is responsible for the airspace above the middle of America, and it spread nationwide."

She also said she received an update from United Airlines, which said, "Air traffic control is limiting the number of planes allowed to land and depart each hour in Los Angeles, affecting several flights. We're monitoring the situation closely to get you to your destination as soon as possible."

Around 6 p.m. ET, she said her flight "going over the Pacific" was finally "pushing back" from the gate. The New York Times has reported that "some international flights from the United States have been allowed to depart amid the ground stop." Alaska Airlines said in a statement that flights within Hawaii and Alaska have also been continuing, as have longer-distance flights to and from Honolulu.

Nationwide ground stops are pretty rare. The last time such an event occurred was in January 2023, when a pilot notification system went down. Before then, a nationwide ground stop was issued following the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Last year Congress approved $12.5 billion to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on, including old copper wires and radio systems. On social media, the GOP-controlled Senate Commerce Committee, which oversees the FAA, noted that "no new" air traffic area control centers have been built "since LBJ was in office." The Trump administration has requested another $30 billion to modernize the nation's air-traffic control system.

articles.title: Caos aéreo: 10 perguntas e respostas sobre a paralisação dos aeroportos nos Estados Unidos | G1
articles.standfirst: Problema de telecomunicações teria motivado suspensão de todas as decolagens no país. Espaço aéreo foi reaberto após 4 horas. Milhares de voos foram cancelados.
articles.summary: Problema de telecomunicações teria motivado suspensão de todas as decolagens no país. Espaço aéreo foi reaberto após 4 horas. Milhares de voos foram cancelados.
articles.body:
A Administração Federal de Aviação dos Estados Unidos (FAA, na sigla em inglês) suspendeu nesta sexta-feira (13), durante 4 horas, as decolagens em todos os aeroportos do país. A medida foi adotada por causa de uma falha nas comunicações dos centros de controle de tráfego aéreo.

Segundo a agência, o problema envolveu os sistemas de telecomunicações usados no controle dos voos. O governo americano investiga as causas, mas o presidente Donald Trump descartou, inicialmente, uma relação com ataques cibernéticos ou com o uso de inteligência artificial.

A paralisação provocou milhares de cancelamentos e atrasos. Mais de 13 mil voos foram afetados, segundo o jornal The Wall Street Journal. Os impactos devem continuar durante o fim de semana, enquanto as companhias reorganizam suas operações.

A suspensão também atingiu voos internacionais com destino aos Estados Unidos. Autoridades do México e da Europa adotaram restrições a pedido da FAA. O episódio foi a segunda paralisação nacional de decolagens nos EUA desde os ataques de 11 de setembro de 2001.

Veja o que se sabe sobre a suspensão de voos nos EUA:

1. O que causou a paralisação dos voos nos EUA?

Ainda não há uma resposta definitiva sobre o que motivou a paralisação. O governo americano afirma que segue apurando os detalhes.

Segundo declaração do secretário de Segurança Interna dos EUA, Markwayne Mullin, um problema de telecomunicações provocou a interrupção das operações.

De acordo com a rede CBS News, a falha teria sido causada por uma atualização na rede operada pela L3Harris, responsável por conectar os sistemas de controle de tráfego aéreo. O problema teria provocado uma interrupção nas comunicações.

Um avião pousa após a Administração Federal de Aviação dos EUA (FAA) emitir uma ordem nacional de suspensão de voos em solo "devido a circunstâncias extraordinárias e razões de segurança". Aeroporto Nacional Ronald Reagan de Washington , em Arlington, Virgínia, EUA — Foto: REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst

2. Quantos voos foram afetados pela suspensão?

Mais de 13 mil voos foram cancelados ou sofreram atrasos por causa da suspensão das decolagens, segundo o jornal americano The Wall Street Journal.

Além disso, mais de 1,5 milhão de passageiros tinham viagens programadas em voos que partiriam depois do início da restrição. A estimativa é da empresa de análise de dados da aviação Cirium, citada pelo The New York Times.

Até as 20h (horário de Brasília), cerca de 600 aeronaves haviam sido desviadas para aeroportos diferentes dos destinos originais. A maioria retornou ao aeroporto de onde havia decolado.

O Aeroporto Internacional O'Hare, em Chicago, registrou o maior número de desvios, com 28 voos. Em seguida, aparece o Aeroporto Internacional de Denver, com 26.

3. A falha afetou toda a frota amaericana?

Não. Apesar da suspensão nacional, alguns voos internacionais com origem nos Estados Unidos conseguiram decolar.

Segundo registros da plataforma de monitoramento aéreo Flightradar24, citados pelo The New York Times, aeronaves que partiram de Boston e Nova York com destino à Europa e à Ásia foram autorizadas a deixar o solo depois de atrasos.

Sim. A restrição teve impacto em operações fora dos Estados Unidos.

A FAA pediu à autoridade de aviação do México que mantivesse em solo aeronaves nos aeroportos mexicanos com voos programados para os Estados Unidos, informou a agência mexicana nesta sexta-feira (13).

Na Europa, a Eurocontrol, organização responsável pela coordenação do tráfego aéreo no continente, suspendeu voos com origem nos países-membros e destino aos Estados Unidos a pedido da FAA. Segundo comunicado da entidade, a decisão foi tomada por causa de problemas técnicos.

5. Qual foi a última vez que aconteceu uma paralisação desse tipo?

A última vez que a Administração Federal de Aviação (FAA) suspendeu todas as decolagens nos Estados Unidos foi em janeiro de 2023.

Na ocasião, uma falha no sistema de informações aeronáuticas da agência provocou o cancelamento de mais de 1.300 voos e atrasos em quase 10 mil.

6. Há alguma suspeita de atentado terrorista?

Não. O secretário de Segurança Interna dos Estados Unidos descartou a possibilidade de ataque e afirmou que o episódio não é um "novo 11 de setembro" e que se trata apenas de uma falha nas telecomunicações.

7. A pane tem a ver com inteligência artificial?

A suspensão das decolagens nos Estados Unidos ocorreu poucos dias depois da FAA ampliar o uso de um sistema de inteligência artificial para auxiliar no controle do tráfego aéreo. A ferramenta, chamada SMART, começou a ser implantada em setembro e chegou aos 22 centros de controle do país em 10 de novembro, segundo a revista especializada Ars Technica.

O sistema analisa dados meteorológicos, rotas de voos e disponibilidade de controladores para sugerir mudanças que reduzam atrasos e melhorem a circulação de aeronaves. As recomendações, porém, continuam sob avaliação de profissionais da agência.

Não há explicação oficial que relacione a ferramenta à paralisação. A empresa Air Space Intelligence, responsável pelo desenvolvimento do sistema, negou envolvimento na falha. O governo americano investiga o caso, cuja hipótese inicial aponta para um problema nas telecomunicações.

8. Este caso tem alguma relação com o problema envolvendo a Microsoft?

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou em entrevista à Fox News que a suspensão dos voos não parece ter relação com um ataque cibernético ou com problemas envolvendo inteligência artificial.

A Microsoft, que enfrentou problemas técnicos na quinta-feira (12), também negou qualquer ligação com o episódio. Em comunicado, a empresa afirmou que "não há nenhuma indicação" de que a suspensão das decolagens esteja relacionada aos serviços da companhia.

Em entrevista à imprensa na Casa Branca, o secretário de Segurança Interna, Markwayne Mullin, também disse que não há "nenhuma razão" para relacionar a paralisação aos problemas tecnológicos envolvendo a Microsoft.

Passageiros aguardam no Aeroporto Internacional Logan após a Administração Federal de Aviação dos EUA (FAA) emitir uma ordem nacional de suspensão de voos em solo "devido a circunstâncias extraordinárias e razões de segurança", na sequência de um relatório anterior da agência sobre graves problemas de comunicação no controle de tráfego aéreo, em East Boston, Massachusetts, EUA, 13 de novembro de 2026 — Foto: Brian Snyder / REUTERS

Até o momento, a FAA não informou quando a suspensão será encerrada. A previsão inicial era que a restrição durasse até as 22h UTC (19h no horário de Brasília).

Segundo o analista de aviação Robert Mann, em entrevista à agência Reuters, se a suspensão continuar até a noite, provavelmente será necessário esperar até o fim de semana para resolver os impactos nas operações das companhias aéreas.

10. O que dizem as autoridades e empresas no Brasil?

A Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac) monitora a situação e recomenda que os passageiros consultem as companhias aéreas para verificar possíveis alterações nos voos.

A agência também orienta as empresas a comunicar imediatamente eventuais atrasos e cancelamentos e a manter os passageiros informados sobre a previsão de partida.

Em caso de atraso ou cancelamento, a reacomodação deve ser gratuita e pode ocorrer no primeiro voo disponível da própria companhia ou de outra empresa.

Se preferir viajar em outra data ou horário, o passageiro pode escolher um voo da própria companhia aérea, respeitado o prazo de validade da passagem.

A GRU Airport recebeu alerta para manter em solo os voos de ou para os EUA até novo aviso e orienta os passageiros a procurarem as companhias aéreas.

A Gol informou que monitora dois voos que partem dos EUA, com foco na segurança. A Azul aguarda orientações. Um voo da companhia seguia normalmente para Orlando, enquanto outros três estavam programados.

A plataforma de inteligência artificial implementada pela Secretaria de Segurança Pública do Estado do Paraná (Sesp) apoiou o esclarecimento de 2,8 mil casos de janeiro até 29 de outubro de 2026. Segundo a Sesp, foram realizadas 2,2 mil prisões com o auxílio da ferramenta e 680 veículos foram recuperados , pelas polícias Militar e Civil do estado. Entenda abaixo como funciona.

Em janeiro, mês da implantação do sistema, 20 casos foram resolvidos com a ajuda a IA e, em setembro, este número saltou para 600 casos, um aumento de 2.900% ou 30 vezes maior. Os dados foram solicitados pelo g1 Paraná e fornecidos pela Sesp.

De acordo com o Tenente-coronel Cleverson Machado, coordenador do Centro Integrado de Controle e Comando (CICCR) Sesp, o uso da ferramenta tem ‘maximizado’ as ações dos policiais.

“O que a gente percebe é uma uma evolução enorme para nós, assim, dia após dia, a gente percebe que o nosso policial está entendendo a ferramenta, nós estamos amadurecendo e não são só os policiais, eu acho que é a sociedade como um todo [...]. A gente busca fazer tudo de uma maneira muito madura, às vezes a gente pode até ser um pouquinho mais lento, alguém pode pensar, mas assim, a gente busca fazer tudo da maneira mais correta possível”, explica Machado.

Centro Integrado de Comando e Controle Regional (CICCR) do Paraná. — Foto: Foto: SESP-PR

A plataforma de Inteligência Artificial da Sesp utiliza uma t ecnologia desenvolvida pela empresa brasileira Pax, que também fornece o serviço para os estados de São Paulo, Goiás e Ceará, e é voltada para a aplicação na segurança pública.

A empresa define a IA como um “assistente de investigação”. Ainda, conta que a tecnologia faz o cruzamento de grande volume de dados e informações, permitindo identificar suspeitos, reconstruir trajetos e localizar veículos “em segundos”.

“O sistema consegue, por exemplo, localizar um veículo mesmo quando não se conhece sua placa, identificar trajetos percorridos por suspeitos, reconhecer padrões de deslocamento e relacionar informações aparentemente desconectadas. Uma característica pouco relevante isoladamente, como a cor de uma roupa, um adesivo ou um detalhe de um automóvel, pode se transformar no ponto de partida para uma investigação”, afirma a Pax.

A empresa destaca ainda que, na prática, o que muda é a velocidade e capacidade de processamento de informações. A responsabilidade de analisar os dados, aprofundar as investigações e realizar prisões continua sendo das forças de segurança pública.

Cruzamento de dados é feito através de IA, no Paraná — Foto: Foto: Sesp

No Paraná, através do programa Olho Vivo, o Governo do Estado instalou, até o momento, cerca de 1 mil câmeras inteligentes, em 21 municípios , segundo a assessoria da Sesp.

Dados da Pax mostram que as cidades do Paraná com mais casos de esclarecimentos com o apoio da ferramenta são: Londrina , Maringá , Foz do Iguaçu , Cascavel e São José dos Pinhais .

A IA faz então a análise das imagens das câmeras de monitoramento no Centro Integrado de Comando e Controle Regional (CICCR) e realiza o cruzamento com os dados da base da Sesp, como mandados de prisão e apreensão, informações sobre furtos e roubos. “Essa IA faz essa compilação mais rápida e há um ‘match’, vamos colocar assim, há uma ligação entre o evento e a situação que está acontecendo”, diz o tenente-coronel.

“Isso é lançado para as equipes mais próximas e essas equipes podem fazer a verificação de uma maneira mais pormenorizada, mais assertiva, do que se eu tivesse que fazer, por exemplo, 10 abordagens em um tipo de veículo. Eu vou saber a direção, a placa, talvez alguma característica daquele veículo, e isso agiliza o meu processo ”, exemplifica ele.

No caso da Polícia Militar, os agentes recebem as informações diretamente em um dispositivo eletrônico mobile, disponível para cada viatura, e seguem o protocolo policial já existente para decidir o que fazer em cada contexto ou abordagem.

O tenente-coronel Machado afirma que a tecnologia de IA é contratada, mas que é a Sesp que administra os dados. “A base de dados de segurança pública é nossa, a titularidade é nossa, a custódia é nossa, então não existe qualquer ação de externos frente aos dados de segurança pública”, diz. “A gente faz questão de deixar isso muito transparente com os nossos tribunais”.

Segundo Machado, as ações dos policiais são auditáveis e verificáveis, pois todos tem logins e senhas de acesso com duplo fator de confirmação.

A empresa Pax frisa que desenvolve a tecnologia, mas “não é dona dos dados e nem tem acesso livre a eles”.

“Os dados ficam sob custódia e controle do poder público. Pela LGPD, o órgão público é o controlador e a Pax é a operadora. Isso quer dizer que a Pax trata os dados só conforme as instruções do órgão e para as finalidades de segurança pública previstas. A Pax nunca comercializa ou reaproveita nenhum dado, e não mantém acervo próprio de informações sobre cidadãos”, informou a empresa ao g1.

Ainda, a empresa conta que o sistema possui várias camadas de proteção, veja:

Dados no Brasil: por obrigação contratual, os dados são armazenados e processados no Brasil, no ambiente de nuvem escolhido pelo órgão público. Parceiros e fornecedores da Pax não podem usar esses dados.

Acesso restrito à função: só acessam a plataforma os profissionais de segurança pública previamente credenciados, sempre com autenticação multifator. As permissões seguem o princípio do mínimo privilégio: cada profissional vê só o que a sua função exige.

Toda busca tem motivo e deixa registro: o acesso é vinculado à finalidade, e o profissional informa a justificativa no momento do uso. Cada ação gera um registro inviolável, que nunca é alterado e nem apagado. Com isso, dá para reconstruir qual agente acessou quais dados e em que momento, o que serve de base para a auditoria de corregedorias e órgãos de controle.

Prazo de guarda definido pelo poder público: ao fim do prazo, os dados são expurgados da plataforma de forma definitiva e irreversível.

Certificação: a Pax é certificada na ISO 27001, a principal norma internacional de gestão de segurança da informação.

Ampliação do projeto foi suspensa pelo TCE e revogada pelo Governo

O Governo do Paraná havia anunciado que o projeto seja ampliado, mas o processo para licitação foi suspenso pelo Tribunal de Contas do Estado do Paraná (TCE-PR), em abril deste ano, por "riscos de sobrepreço, exposição de dados pessoais e violação de direitos fundamentais" apontados pelos auditores do TCE-PR.

Em outubro, o Governo do Paraná informou que revogou a licitação com pregão de R$ 581 milhões, que previa a aquisição de cerca de 20 mil câmeras e a contratação de uma empresa para a integração dos equipamentos aos sistemas de segurança, com o objetivo de ampliar a cobertura do programa.

Segundo a justificativa apresentada em Diário Oficial, a revogação da licitação se deu pela evolução das tecnologias de videomonitoramento e integração de dados, a proximidade do fim do mandato do atual governo e a necessidade de que a próxima gestão avalie o projeto e a disponibilidade orçamentária antes de assumir o compromisso financeiro de longo prazo.

articles.title: Suspensão de voos nos EUA afeta Brasil e gera caos nos aeroportos | G1
articles.standfirst: Interrupção do tráfego aéreo por cerca de quatro horas deve demorar muitas horas para descongestionar os voos atrasados e cancelados desta sexta-feira (13). Em SP, 15 voos foram afetados até 0h.
articles.summary: Com mais de 10 mil voos atrasados por falha de rádio, a suspensão de voos nos EUA sobrecarrega trens e afeta operações no Brasil, exigindo dias para normalização.
articles.body:
Passageiros aguardam no Aeroporto Internacional Logan após a Administração Federal de Aviação dos EUA (FAA) emitir uma ordem nacional de suspensão de voos em solo "devido a circunstâncias extraordinárias e razões de segurança", na sequência de um relatório anterior da agência sobre graves problemas de comunicação no controle de tráfego aéreo, em East Boston, Massachusetts, EUA, 13 de novembro de 2026 — Foto: Brian Snyder / REUTERS

A paralisação total dos aeroportos dos Estados Unidos , ocorrida por aproximadamente quatro horas na noite desta sexta-feira (13), gerou um efeito cascata tanto no país quanto em todo o mundo, inclusive no Brasil. Os serviços foram retomados às 22h20 no horário de Brasília .

A Administração Federal de Aviação dos Estados Unidos tomou a medida rara de parar todos os voos no país, a segunda desde os ataques de 11 de Setembro de 2001, por uma conta de uma falha de comunicação (leia mais abaixo) .

Os Estados Unidos são o maior mercado de passageiros do mundo. Em 2025, foram registrados 890,1 milhões de passageiros, considerando chegadas e partidas, segundo dados da Associação Internacional de Transporte Aéreo (IATA, na siga em inglês).

Dentro dos Estados Unidos, os trens ficaram sobrecarregados com a demanda de passageiros em busca de alternativas sem a possibilidade de voarem. Ocorreram picos de buscas por reservas, segundo a Amtrak, empresa federal responsável pelo serviço de trens nacionais.

Mais de 10 mil voos estão atrasados ou foram cancelados, segundo o site de monitoramento FlightAware. A FAA ainda não deu previsão, mas retirou a suspensão nacional das decolagens por volta de 22h20 (de Brasília).

O secretário de Segurança Interna dos Estados Unidos, Markwayne Mullin, afirmou que o governo não tem indícios de que a interrupção tenha sido provocada por um ataque. Segundo ele, o problema está relacionado a uma falha temporária nos serviços de telecomunicações.

A TV Globo apurou com uma fonte que trabalha em uma torre de controle de um aeroporto de Nova York que o problema está relacionado a um cruzamento de frequências de rádio.

Com isso, mais de uma aeronave consegue transmitir mensagens ao mesmo tempo na mesma frequência, o que dificulta a comunicação com os controladores. Na prática, os profissionais não conseguem identificar com clareza qual avião está falando com a torre.

"Se a suspensão das decolagens continuar até a noite, provavelmente será necessário esperar até o fim de semana para resolver os impactos nas operações das companhias aéreas", afirmou Robert Mann, analista de aviação e diretor da consultoria R.W. Mann & Co, à Reuters, antes de a suspensão ser retirada e os aeroportos serem reabertos.

👉 Alguns voos internacionais com origem nos Estados Unidos foram autorizados a decolar mesmo durante a suspensão nacional das operações, segundo o site de monitoramento aéreo Flightradar24. Aeronaves que partiram de Boston e Nova York com destino à Europa e à Ásia conseguiram decolar após atrasos, de acordo com os registros da plataforma, citados pelo jornal The New York Times.

No Brasil, a Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac) informou que monitorou a situação dos voos paralisados nos EUA e recomendou aos passageiros que busquem as companhias aéreas para verificar a situação do voo ou eventuais alterações.

O fechamento dos aeroportos americanos afetou voos de outros países com destino aos EUA. Foram 15 voos somente do Aeroporto Internacional de Guarulhos, o aeroporto mais movimentado do Brasil, entre as decolagens previstas até 0h.

Destes 15 voos, quatro foram cancelados, dois estavam atrasados e nove confirmados até a atualização mais recente da gestora do aeroporto, feita às 21h30 desta sexta.

A Eurocontrol, organização responsável pela coordenação do tráfego aéreo na Europa, informou que suspendeu todo o tráfego com origem em países-membros e destino a aeroportos dos Estados Unidos, a pedido da FAA

O secretário de Transportes dos Estados Unidos, Sean Duffy, afirmou que a falha atingiu todos os centros de controle responsáveis pelo tráfego nas rotas aéreas do país. Técnicos da FAA investigam o problema, segundo ele.

A Microsoft, que enfrentou problemas técnicos nesta quinta-feira (12), afirma que "não há nenhuma indicação" que a suspensão dos voos nos EUA tenha relação com os serviços da empresa.

A Bloomberg informou que o FBI não acredita que o problema de comunicação tenha sido causado por um ataque cibernético ou uma ação criminosa.

Segundo a agência de notícias, a polícia americana investiga se uma atualização de software pode ter provocado a falha nos sistemas da FAA.

Mapa de aviões no espaço aéreo dos EUA — Foto: Reprodução/Flightradar24

O episódio ocorreu em meio a uma série de problemas no sistema de controle de tráfego aéreo dos Estados Unidos, que enfrenta falhas em equipamentos, problemas de comunicação e falta de controladores.

O governo tenta modernizar a estrutura, que está envelhecida. No ano passado, o Congresso aprovou US$ 12,5 bilhões para a reforma do sistema. Nesta sexta-feira (13), a FAA e a Casa Branca pediram aos parlamentares mais US$ 30,1 bilhões para resolver outros problemas.

articles.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
articles.summary: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.
articles.body:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.

Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.

Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".

"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.

Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.

Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says.

Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.

"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."

King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.

"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."

African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.

But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.

In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.

It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.

"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.

"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."

Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.

The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.

And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".

But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.

No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.

Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.

These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.

The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".

The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.

"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.

And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.

"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.

Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."

Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."

But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.

Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.

"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."

That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.

"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.

"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Police launch investigation' into Walliams and Piddington asylum 'betrayal'
articles.summary: An investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences" leads a number of Saturday's papers.
articles.body:
Many of Saturday's papers lead with the Metropolitan Police launching an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences". The Guardian - which published a report detailing separate allegations on Tuesday - reminds readers that the comedian and children's author has denied any wrongdoing, being a sexual predator or breaking the law. The Daily Mail reports that fans are deserting him.

The Sun refers to the jailing earlier this week of the comedian Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault. The co-host of the Great British Bake-Off, Noel Fielding, tells the paper of his "shame" at vile jokes he once made with Brand and stresses that they were "never pals" nor did he know of Brand's crimes.

"We will fight this betrayal," is the defiant message in the Daily Express from residents of Piddington , Oxfordshire - where the government has granted planning permission for the use of a former military site to house more than 1,200 asylum seekers. The paper says Home Office sources believe it will create a fairer distribution of asylum seekers. But it reports that locals have warned the government to brace for a legal battle.

The Guardian raises questions about Reform UK leader Nigel Farage's claims that he used a £5m gift for his personal security. It says sources have told the paper his personal security has been paid for out of the party's central funds. A party spokesperson tells the Guardian that "as a standard practice, we do not comment on security matters".

The Daily Mirror says Friday's "Microsoft meltdown" caused "utter chaos" for millions of email users around the world. The Daily Telegraph 's cartoonist Matt takes a wry look at the outage, depicting a man standing outside a house and shouting up to its resident: "Microsoft emails aren't working. You purchased something from our shop four years ago and we wanted to tell you about our exciting new offers."

There is a common theme to coverage of Mauricio Pochettino leaving his role as head of the USA national football team to take the top job at Manchester United. "Ready and wailing", suggests the Daily Express. It was a "tearful farewell", according to the Times . The Daily Star says he was in tears - "and he hasn't even started yet".

images.caption: Saturday's Daily Mirror is one of a number of papers leading on the Metropolitan Police launching an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences". The force said it was investigating allegations which were separate to those reported by ITV News and the Guardian earlier this week, but that detectives were also "proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences". Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law" after those allegations were first reported.

articles.title: UK weather: Frost and freezing fog forecast as cold health alerts continue
articles.summary: It's a weekend of two halves with a cold start on Saturday giving way to wetter and milder day on Sunday.
articles.body:
Arctic air will maintain its grip on the UK to start the weekend, as cold health alerts remain in place for a large swathe of England.

Saturday will dawn with another sharp and widespread frost with the coldest conditions expected in England and Wales.

Patches of freezing fog could also be a hazard, reducing visibility and bringing a risk of very slippery surfaces in southern and eastern England.

Then it is all change by Sunday with most areas having a frost-free start, but heavy bursts of rain and brisk winds will sweep across the country later.

Freezing fog could cause some disruption on Saturday

Saturday will start with temperatures widely below freezing in parts of England and Wales.

Lows in towns and cities are expected to fall to -2 or -3C, but in the countryside they could be as low as -5C.

In southern and south-east England there could also be some patchy freezing fog which forms in air that is below freezing.

Super-cooled water droplets remain suspended in the air and it can be particularly dangerous as they can freeze on impact turning untreated pavements into instant ice rinks.

Yellow cold health alerts from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) are in force for the West Midlands and north-west England until 12:00 Saturday , external .

More of a breeze further north will mean most places will be a few degrees above freezing.

After the fog and frost clears, Saturday will largely become a bright and dry day.

By the afternoon, temperatures will rise across the UK - ranging from 7C in parts of the Highlands to a milder 12C in south-west England.

England and Wales are forecast to see long spells of sunshine, away from the odd shower early on in the far north-west.

Northern Ireland will have some bright spells in the morning, with thickening cloud in the afternoon and rain by evening.

A few showers are expected in parts of Scotland where is will also be a breezy day, and will feel colder due to the wind chill .

The chilly but mainly dry spell of late will be replaced by something more unsettled on Sunday as low pressure sweeps in from the Atlantic.

Areas of showery rain will drift from west to east across much of the UK.

The heaviest of the rain is likely in Scotland and Northern Ireland, as well as southern and western parts of England and Wales.

This is generally good news for places still suffering from drought or severe drought , although parts of eastern England may avoid most of the rainfall.

You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app .

articles.title: UK police open sex offence probe into comedian and author David Walliams
articles.summary: The British TV personality, 55, denies sexual assault allegations, saying he has not broken the law.
articles.body:
London’s police have opened an investigation into allegations of serious sexual offences after media reports accused British comedian and children’s author David Walliams of grooming and sexually abusing girls and young women.

The Metropolitan Police said in a statement on Friday that it “has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s”.

In the statement, Met Police Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney urged anyone affected to come forward.

The Met said the new allegations are separate from those reported this week by ITV News and The Guardian.

The two news organisations published reports on Tuesday that several women had accused Walliams of sexual misconduct, with the allegations dating back as far as 2003.

The reports came out a day after comedian Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for rape and sexual assault.

The Guardian and ITV said they spoke to more than 100 people during a three-year investigation.

One woman said Walliams sexually assaulted her at his London home when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them as teenagers. The reports also included allegations that he harassed young female colleagues.

In a letter to ITV and The Guardian, he said: “Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

He added: “I am not a sexual predator … I have not broken the law.”

The investigative reports were published after he lost a High Court bid to block the media outlets from naming him.

The judge, Matthew Nicklin, said an injunction would be “an exceptionally serious interference” with the media’s rights.

A spokesperson for the BBC told the AFP news agency that it had taken down some shows involving Walliams, including all episodes of Little Britain, the comedy sketch show that made him famous.

His literary agency, Independent Talent Group, said it was “no longer representing him in any capacity”.

Walliams’s publisher, HarperCollins, dropped him last year, following accusations that he harassed female staff, which he had also denied.

Walliams rose to fame as a comedian with sketch shows Little Britain and Come Fly With Me. He was also a judge on ITV’s Britain’s Got Talent.

He penned children’s books that have reportedly sold more than 50 million copies, including Mr Stink, Gangsta Granny and The Boy in the Dress.

articles.title: Christmas trees: How early is too early to buy one and will it last until Christmas?
articles.summary: Supermarkets have started selling Christmas trees - six weeks out from the big day.
articles.body:
The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner plate. Some might feel the best time is just after Bonfire Night, others may think Christmas Eve is more apt, and most will probably plump for somewhere in between.

Tesco started selling Christmas trees at half-price this week and said more than 90% of its trees had sold out by the end of November last year.

Lidl and some other retailers are also launching their ranges next week, while others including Dobbies Garden Centres are waiting until the last week of November.

But with Christmas Day still six weeks away, is it unwise to rush into buying a real tree so early? And do you risk spending your Christmas week cleaning up piles of pine needles?

Probably, says Mick Walker, from Bolton Christmas Trees, which grows trees in the Scottish Highlands before sending them to homes across the UK.

"It might last until the beginning of Christmas, but it won't last the full holiday," he warns. "Unless its a potted one, it's going to be sagging by Christmas Day - big time."

He calls Tesco's half-price deal "insane", adding that it's "sucking them into buying something now that isn't going to do the job".

So when would he suggest is the best time? "If it was me, I'd put it up a week before Christmas eve, [and it will] last straight through until New Year."

According to the Royal Horticultural Society, cut Christmas trees should usually last about four weeks with the right care - although some retailers suggest their trees can last between four and six weeks.

Tesco told the BBC its range includes both cut firs as well as potted spruces and firs, but that all its trees have care instructions on the labels that should "keep them looking their best right up until Christmas Day".

They encourage any customer who buys a product they aren't happy with to return it to the store.

Walker has some practical tips to keep your tree looking good for as long as possible this Christmas.

"Keep watering it, spraying the leaves, keeping it cool, keeping it away from radiators in the coolest spot in the room," he says.

In addition to Walker's tips, Forestry England also recommends giving your tree's trunk a trim when you get it home. Sawing off around half an inch (1.2cm) from the base will rid your tree of any hardened sap, allowing it to absorb more water, it says.

And have you heard the one about using cola or corn syrup in the base to help keep your tree alive? It's a myth, tree experts say.

"Your beautiful tree just wants a constant supply of fresh water - it's that simple," Forestry England states on its website .

Forester Richard Cooper, from Forestry England, tells the BBC that keeping a cut tree outside in a shaded area might help prolong its life. However, he adds: "It depends how keen you are to get it up and decorated."

Keeping a potted tree outside and bringing it indoors for Christmas each year is also an option if you have the outdoor space, he says.

But trees in pots should be brought indoors "as late as possible - the weekend before Christmas is ideal", advises the RHS.

"Do not keep living trees in the house any longer than 12 days but be guided by the tree. If it looks unhappy, put it back outside."

The most popular Christmas trees available in the UK are the Nordmann fir variety, which are non-drop, meaning they don't drop their needles. Norway Spruce is another common variety and have a strong pine scent, but generally should be kept outdoors or put up just before Christmas.

Pine trees, Walker says, have the longest lifespan, but he concedes they lack that classic Christmas look.

Or, of course, you could opt for a tried-and-tested artificial tree, which is what Katie McDonald from Belfast put up in her house last week.

"When I was a kid my mum always waited to the last minute to let us kids put the tree up. We would be the last house on our street and the last of all our friends to get the tree up," she tells the BBC.

"So I made myself a wee childlike promise that when I had my own house I'd be one of the first to put my tree up."

She says she will replace her artificial tree with a real one in a few weeks, so it is in prime condition come Christmas Day.

Meanwhile, Steve Chapman, from Merseyside, told the BBC the festive season for his family is all about traditions, and while his kids wouldn't settle for just 12 days of Christmas, "it's certainly not two months of Christmas".

His family always try to avoid the urge to decorate too soon, so in the first week of December they head down to a local farm that grows Christmas trees. They will select one from the field and have it delivered the same day.

"There is nothing better than the smell of a real tree at Christmas," Steve says.

articles.body: More than 700 flights within, into and out of the United States were cancelled on Saturday following a nationwide ground stop imposed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) a day earlier due to a telecommunications outage affecting air traffic control centres.According to flight data tracker FlightAware, as of 7.45 pm ET, Delta Air Lines had cancelled 5 per cent of its flights, United Airlines 4 per cent and American Airlines 2 per cent.Air Canada has cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of Friday evening due to the ongoing FAA ground stop.The outage appears to have affected a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to two airline officials and a US official. The network handles critical radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers to communicate with pilots.The FAA grounded all flights nationwide on Friday afternoon after communications problems affected regional air traffic control centres. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the centres, which direct planes between airports across the country, were experiencing a communications issue and that FAA technicians were investigating.Some flights have since been cleared for departure, including services within Alaska and Hawaii, as well as certain international flights departing US airspace.US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the disruption was unlikely to have been caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence, as authorities continued to investigate the outage.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said there was no indication that the disruption was linked to a national security threat, although he did not rule out any possible cause, including a cyberattack."This isn’t the same comparison to 9/11," Mullin told reporters outside the White House, adding that all flights had been accounted for and passengers were safe. He said there was no indication that the incident was a hostile attack against the country."It’s just a telecommunications outage," he said.The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a malfunction in a key FAA computer system disrupted flights. Before that, the last such shutdown had followed the September 11, 2001, attacks.The disruption also affected travel plans for several sports teams, with multiple NBA, NHL and college teams left stranded ahead of a busy weekend of sporting events. And when he comes to you, ask your question. But if you're just yelling over the other guy's question, a louder, different question. That s---'s annoying." Rogan contrasted this with David Sacks, chairman of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, recalling Sacks' complaint that the administration had lost the podcasters with recent policies and ought to have given them a front-row seat at news conferences. articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi to meet in first trilateral meeting between leaders
articles.summary: President Trump plans to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next week, marking the first-ever trilateral meeting between the three leaders. Trump will be in Asia for The Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippines and…
articles.body:
President Trump plans to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next week, marking the first-ever trilateral meeting between the three leaders.

Trump will be in Asia for The Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippines and the APEC summit in China.

“The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesman, told reporters.

A senior U.S. official said that no agreement is expected to come of the meeting.

“I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level, between these countries,” the official said, adding that it’s “hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”

The official noted that Iran will also be a topic of discussion but notably said that the president does not intend to discuss Ukraine.

Trump had suggested earlier this month that he would be having a meeting with Putin and Xi, but it hadn’t been confirmed until now.

The last nuclear arms pact between the U.S. and Russia, the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), expired in February. The treaty had been extended for five years under the Biden administration and capped the number of deployed strategic warheads and deployed launchers the U.S. and Russia could have.

New START could not be extended again, so Trump would need to negotiate a new treaty.

“If it expires, it expires. We’ll do a better agreement,” Trump said in January.

articles.title: What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stoppage since 9/11
articles.summary: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack or a Microsoft outage.
articles.body:
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.

The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.

The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.

The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.

The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.

All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.

There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.

Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.

Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.

"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.

Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.

Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations.

American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning.

Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.

"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.

He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag.

"It's going to continue to fail," he said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.

He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.

Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.

Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.

It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.

"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.

Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.

"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.

The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.

But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

articles.title: FAA ground stop lifted: Why were US flights grounded, and what’s next?
articles.summary: The FAA says nationwide ground stop disrupting thousands of US flights was caused by a telecommunications outage.
articles.body:
The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop imposed on Friday that halted departing flights, an order it issued citing “extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety”.

The halt, which grounded thousands of flights across the country, was lifted on Friday evening after five hours, making it the longest ground stop in 25 years.

It was also the second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11, 2001, attacks.

“Everybody’s safe,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, adding that this was not “another 9/11” and that there were no suspected cyberattacks.

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54pm Eastern Time (20:54 GMT) on Friday due to a telecommunications outage affecting air route traffic control centres, which handle flights travelling across the country.

The FAA confirmed that the nationwide ground stop had been lifted.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said airspace reopened at 8:15pm ET (01:15 GMT on Saturday), after more than four hours of disruption.

“We’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said, warning that flights would not resume immediately.

“It’s going to be slow,” he added, urging passengers to check with their airlines.

Duffy said flights would resume depending on the availability of pilots and flight attendants, with authorities trying to get as many flights moving as possible on Friday night.

Aviation analytics firm Cirium said that after 4pm ET (21:00 GMT) on Friday, about 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were still scheduled to depart from US airports.

By 7:05pm ET (00:05 GMT on Saturday), at least 827 flights had been diverted, according to Cirium. Of those, 670 returned to their departure airports, while 157 were diverted elsewhere.

Aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land during the ground stop.

During the ground stop, international flights were handled on a case-by-case basis, with some allowed to depart despite the restrictions.

More than 4,700 flights were cancelled and 10,000 delayed on Friday, while another 700 had already been cancelled for Saturday, according to FlightRadar24.

Aviation analysts said it could take days for airlines to restore their schedules.

Reporting from Los Angeles international airport, Al Jazeera’s John Hendren spoke to passenger Nicholas Erdodi, who travelled from New Zealand and was trying to reach Chicago for a conference.

Erdodi said he had been travelling for 16 to 18 hours before spending another six hours at the airport, where passengers had been forced to leave their plane.

“The challenge is you cannot ask anyone here what to do,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Lack of information is what bothers me, I mean, and not to mention find the hotel for the night, not to mention all the cost.”

Erdodi said he had been rebooked but remained uncertain whether his next flight would depart.

“I work in tech, I understand what could be going on, but someone needs to tell us,” he said.

“It doesn’t matter if someone tells us that we don’t know what’s happening, but please just let us know what’s going on,” he added.

What does a nationwide ground stop mean?

A nationwide ground stop temporarily requires departing aircraft to remain on the ground until cleared to take off.

Flights in the air are generally allowed to continue to their destination, but new departures are on strict orders to stay grounded.

The measure is intended to stop any further aircraft from entering the airspace as the authorities deal with the safety issues.

What caused the FAA nationwide ground stop?

The FAA said the ground stop was caused by a telecommunications outage affecting air traffic control systems.

Duffy said the outage was caused by switches and routers that became overloaded with data and went down, adding that the incident did not involve a total loss of communications or radar capabilities.

Tony Stanton, a former senior executive with Australia’s Civil Aviation Safety Authority, told Al Jazeera that a US government report published in September warned about problems with the aviation infrastructure before these latest disruptions.

The report , from the Government Accountability Office (GAO), highlighted ageing copper cables dating back to the 1960s and warned that delays in modernising the system could lead to further disruptions.

It also noted that while the FAA was trying to implement changes, officials were prioritising speeding up the process and failing to properly schedule changes, meaning switches were often happening at the same time and overwhelming the system.

On Friday, officials admitted that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps.

Todd Curtis, an aviation safety expert and chief executive of AirSafe.com, told Al Jazeera that the failures appeared to be concentrated in the country’s air route traffic control centres.

“There are 21 across the United States, one in Alaska and the other 20 in the lower 48,” he said.

“These are the folks who handle the aircraft that are transiting from one part of the country to the other, and they rely on multiple handoffs between controllers.”

Speaking before Duffy provided further details, Ron Bartsch, a professor of international aviation law at the University of the South Pacific, raised questions about the apparent failure of backup systems.

“The whole aviation community is based on redundancy,” he told Al Jazeera.

“So the fact that a redundant system hasn’t kicked in immediately just raises more questions than what we’ve seen answers to at this stage.”

Mullin said that there was no cyberattack linked to the nationwide ground stop and that the public was never in danger.

Duffy acknowledged that tens of thousands of travellers had been stranded and called for $50bn in upgrades to the nation’s air traffic control system.

About 3,000 flights have safely landed following the order, Mullin said.

But Duffy warned that it will “take us some time to get back to capacity”, but he expected operations to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving”.

The Thanksgiving travel period, which begins in less than two weeks, is usually one of the busiest times of the year for air travel in the US.

Aviation safety expert Curtis also warned that the disruption could continue affecting passengers even after the technical problems were resolved.

“If it’s fully resolved, it would take more than a day to get back to normal, to reschedule aircraft,” he told Al Jazeera.

He explained that many airlines operate interconnected networks, meaning passengers often have to change planes at major hubs.

“So there could be a bit of a hassle on the part of the airlines trying to figure out how to get everyone to where they have to go,” he said.

Passengers have been advised to check their flight status directly with their airlines, as delays and cancellations might continue.

Could another nationwide ground stop happen?

Experts warn that the ageing US air traffic control system is still very much susceptible to further disruption.

Duffy acknowledged the ageing infrastructure.

“We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded,” he said.

Stanton, the aviation expert, questioned why officials said they did not anticipate an outage when risks were identified.

“That’s incredibly surprising to me when there was a report published only in September that absolutely talked to this risk at hand that we’re seeing today,” he said.

He added that the FAA needed better contingency plans to prevent future technical failures from causing disruption.

“These are things that can be foreseen, can be anticipated, and we should have plans in place so that the system has a minor impact rather than the major impact we’re seeing today,” Stanton said.

articles.summary: Parliament passes legislation months after a thwarted attack at Leipzig-Halle airport, which Berlin linked to Russia.
articles.body:
Germany’s parliament has approved sweeping new powers for the country’s intelligence agencies, allowing them to hack and disrupt adversaries under specified conditions as the government seeks to counter espionage and cyberattacks.

The Bundestag passed the legislation on Friday by 308 votes to 190, with 71 abstentions. The governing Christian Democrats and Social Democrats backed the reform, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and Die Linke, or the Left Party, opposed it.

The changes expand the role of Germany’s foreign intelligence agency, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and its domestic intelligence service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), beyond gathering and analysing information to actively disrupting certain threats.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the legislation as a “reform of the century”, arguing that Germany needed stronger intelligence services to confront terrorism and hostile foreign operations.

The government says the reform addresses a gap in Germany’s security system, as intelligence agencies to date could sometimes identify a threat but lacked the authority to intervene, including when no other agency was responsible or able to act.

Under the new framework, the BfV would be able to take technical measures against serious threats, such as deleting stolen information from an attacker’s server.

For the BND, the expanded operational powers would allow interventions against threats abroad, including disrupting the servers used by state-backed hackers.

Russia accused of attempting drone attack

The approval comes just months after German authorities found an explosive-laden drone near a cargo plane belonging to the Ukrainian firm Antonov Airlines at Leipzig-Halle airport in August, linking the incident to Moscow.

Berlin formally accused Russia of attempting an attack at the state-owned facility, with Dobrindt saying Germany’s intelligence community had determined that a drone discovered at the airport was consistent with Russian technology.

Russia denied involvement, but the accusation led to the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House, a cultural centre, in Berlin. Moscow responded by ordering the closure of a German consulate in St Petersburg and the Goethe-Institut.

“The reform is a direct result of the Zeitenwende [epochal change] and closely tied to Germany’s foreign policy challenges since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022,” Florian Bigge, programme director at think tank Korber-Stiftung, told Al Jazeera.

Bigge said the BND had publicly sought expanded powers since 2024 and that the approval came amid an “increasingly uncertain international order”.

“The security reality has changed fundamentally in recent years,” Bigge said, adding that “Russia is the main trigger: sabotage, cyberattacks and drones. Plus fear of US unpredictability and reduced US intelligence sharing.”

Dobrindt said Friday’s approved changes put German agencies on an equal footing with their European partners.

During previous parliamentary debates, ministers argued that the BND should not have to stand by when other authorities cannot avert a particularly serious threat, while experts speaking to the Bundestag said Berlin’s capabilities “lack modern intervention powers” compared with their Western counterparts.

Still, the reform has drawn objections from opposition lawmakers, particularly Die Linke, who expressed concern about privacy and the historic separation between intelligence gathering and police work.

In a parliamentary motion opposing the bill, Die Linke argued that key provisions failed to meet constitutional standards for intrusive surveillance. The party has warned that the sweeping powers would effectively create a German secret police force, a prospect with particular historical resonance for citizens who lived under the Stasi, East Germany’s secret police between 1950 and 1990.

In September, Die Linke won the Berlin city-state parliament election with 25.7 percent of the vote, allowing the party to appoint a mayor after forming a coalition government.

Thus far, criticism has come from lawmakers and civil liberties groups, Bigge said, adding that “a broader public debate may still come” as the state expands what it can do abroad.

“Germans want more engagement,” Bigge said, but caveated that “they mean diplomacy”.

The main provisions are scheduled to take effect on December 31, pending completion of the legislative process.
